Foreword

A'la Hadrat Imaam Ahmad Raza Khan ie ii 45) - upon whom be mercy - had a great
amount of knowledge and insight into the sciences of the Holy Qur'aan. His translation of the
Holy Qur'aan titled Kanz-ul-Iman fi Tarjama-til-Qur'aan stands out as the most brilliant
translation of the Holy Qur'aan in the Urdu language. A'‘la Hadrat did not write a Tafseer
(Qur'anic commentary) of the entire Holy Qur'aan but his mastery in this field can be
understood by his explanation of Surah al-Duha at the blessed 'Urs of Muhibb al-Rasool
Hadrat Maulana Shah ‘Abd al-Qaadir which took him 6 hours (from 9 AM till 3 PM).

Kanz-ul-Iman fi Tarjama-til-Qur'aan is a beautiful combination of a word-by-word,
conceptual and idiomatic translation, A'la Hadrat kept the translation in accordance with the
high standards of the classical Arabic language.

The method adopted in the translation of Kanz-ul-Iman

I tried my level best to use simple words of the English language in the translation of
Kanz-ul-Iman, without compromising the language itself, so that most people are
able to understand it. However, in order to preserve the exact meanings of Kanz-ul-
Iman - after extensive consultation with people of knowledge - I did compromise on
some of my linguistic preferences.

I tried to use those English words and phrases which are commonly used in the
English-speaking world, so that the translation of Kanz-ul-Iman can be understood
easily all over the world, by as many peopleas possible.

A'la Hadrat's translation is not entirely a word-by-word translation of the Arabic text
of the Holy Qur'aan, rather it is a conceptual and idiomatic translation, supported by
authentic Tafseers (Qur'anic commentaries), coupled with word-by-word
translations. Therefore, the focus throughout my working on this project was to
capture the conceptual understanding of the Holy Qur'aan as presented by Sayyidi
A'la Hadrat. In the process of this translation, I remained committed to translate
what A'la Hadrat had written in the Urdu language and not translate from the Arabic
text of the Holy Qur'aan directly, This befits the claim that I have attempted to
translate Kanz-ul-Iman and not the Arabic text of the Qur'aan itself.

www.dawateislami.net

Explanatory notes have been placed in brackets in case the meaning cannot be *,
properly understood by the reader or if there is a possibility of misunderstanding a
particular meaning.

‘This translation of Kanz-ul-Iman was proofread once in South Africa by an English-
speaking, South African born, highly educated brother. The second proofreading
was done in the U.K. by an English-speaking, U.K. born, highly educated brother.
Thereafter, a copy was placed on the Dawat-e-Islami website for public comment.
The dear and respected Mufti Muhammad Qaasim (author of Tafseer Sirat-ul-Jinan)
also read this translation in detail and gave his valuable input. After reviewing the
input of Mufti Muhammad Qaasim, various other respected scholars and the
comments posted on the Dawat-e-Islami website, the final editing was concluded on
the 25th of Safar-ul-Muzaffar 1442 AH,

When translating Kanz-ul-Iman, I viewed many Urdu and English translations of
the Arabic text of the Holy Qur'aan as well as other translations of Kanz-ul-Iman;
therefore, much care anda great amount ofanalysis has gone into this translation.

May Allah Almighty accept this humble effort and reward all those who assisted in this
translation.

In the service of Deen
Abdun Nabi Hamidi Qaadiri Attaari

Rumooz Awgaaf Qur'aan Majeed

(he jeilez dined: signs of stop nd. pause in the Holy Chis ain

Native speakers of a language pause at some points of their speech and do
not pause at all at some other points; sometimes they make a short pause
and sometimes they make slightly longer pause. It is indeed important to
make pause and not making it at different stages of speech in order to
convey and draw the intended messages correctly. The transcript of the
Holy Qur'aan is in the form of speech, hence the Islamic Scholars have
established the signs for pausing and not accordingly which are called
Rumooz Awgqaaf Qur'aan Majeed. It is essential to abide by these signs
during the recitation of the Noble Qur'aan. They are described below:

A small circle is shown wherever a verse completes. This sign is
in fact a circular ~ which is written as '. It is the symbol of cr’:
(a complete stop) and one should pause at it. Nowadays 's'is not
written; instead a small circle is shown. This symbol is termed as
an Ayah (verse).

This is the sign of ¢/J*s(a necessary stop), one should pause at it;
otherwise, there isa risk that the message might alter altogether.

www.dawateislami.net

This is the sign of FY: (a general stop). It is better to pause at

it. This sign is shown where one's message is not yet complete
and he is about to say more.

This is the sign of 7¢: (a permissible stop). It is better to pause
here and omitting the pause is also permissible.

This is the sign of i% 35. Not pausing at it is preferable.

This is the sign of U” »—3;. Here one should continue recitation
without interruption; however, if someone makes a pause due to
being exhausted, he is exempted. It should be noted that
omitting the pause is more preferable in case of 'U” as compared

to's.

This is the short form of (sisi. It is preferable to continue

reciting without a pause.

This is the short form of Shut one should not pause at it.

This is the sign of U“y4. Sometimes a pause is made at it and

sometimes not. However, it is preferable to pause at it.

It is the word 3, It means ‘stop’. This sign is used where there isa
risk that the reciter will continue to recite at the same place.

www.dawateislami.net

Both of these are the signs of ‘halt’. One should make a short pause
at the sign stopping the voice but not the breath.

This is the sign of a ‘longer halt’. One should pause at it a little
longer than «<____.. But the breath should not break here too. The
difference between a. and «#, is that in case of as., the pause should

bea little longer than that in <<.

Itis the sign of negation. At some places, the sign is shown upon the
symbol of a verse and sometimes within the text. If it is present
within the text, one should never pause at it. In case it is present

above the symbol of the verse [Ol], there is a difference of opinion;

some scholars advise to pause and some advise otherwise.
However, it does not affect the meaning whether one pauses or not
in this case. But the pause should be omitted when this sign is
within the text.

It is the sign for 4, which means that the preceding sign shall also
apply here.

Ifa text lies within the set of the three dots, the reader is allowed to
pause at the first sign of the three dots and continue without
pausing at the next three dots or vice versa. This type of text is
called Mu'aanagah or Muraagabah.

Introduction to Translation Department
(Dawat-e-Islami)

Dawat-e-Islami - the global and non-political religious movement for the
preaching of Quran and Sunnah - has set up about more than one hundred
departments and the Translation Department of Dawat-e-Islami is one of them.
The formation of the Translation Department is aimed at rendering Maktaba-tul-
Madinah's books, booklets, books of other Islamic scholars of Ahl Al-Sunnah,
monthly magazine ‘Faizan-e-Madinah’, and speeches into different foreign languages
so that Islamic teachings can be disseminated worldwide.

The translation of Islamic writings needs a thorough knowledge of Shari'ah in
addition to language skills. Therefore, the Translation Department of Dawat-e-
Islami has adopted the approach of critical 'Shar'i Scrutiny’ of its translation so that
Shari mistakes can be avoided. After the initial translation is completed, the
translation is reviewed from Shar'i point of view. Furthermore, translators are also
provided with the facility of Shar'i guidance from 'Ulamas and Muftis.

Since English is deemed to be the lingua franca in many parts of the world, the
Translation Department has given greater emphasis to the English translation so that
more and more people can be benefitted. More than four thousand books, booklets
and speeches have been translated into 37 languages to date and can be downloaded
for free from the website: www.dawateislami-net. Besides the English language,
translation is also being done into various other languages of the world including
Arabic, French, Chinese, Russian, German, Italian, Spanish and Turkish, ete.

May Allah Almighty bless the Translation Department of Dawat-e-Islami with
eternal success! May the endeavours of this department become a means of eternal
reward for every Islamic brother and sister who makes their contribution to this
great cause!
